gap: The paper says the scan order may be arbitrary; the code must pick one.
rationale: Algorithm 1 and Table 2 are written for the given scan order; no sorting is specified.
quote: BCE fixes an arbitrary order x1, . . . , xn of the chips and scans it once.

gap: Whether a restart with p=⊥ or a backtrack counts as a test.
rationale: Theorem 7 says each iteration performs at most one test, namely Test(p, xi), and O(1) stack operations; restarts perform no test.
quote: Each iteration i = 2, . . . , n performs at most one test, namely Test(p, xi), and O(1) stack operations.

gap: How to simulate 'arbitrary adversarial' bad-chip answers, especially for exhaustive verification.
options: enumerate every Table-1-allowed verdict pair and every adaptive branch
chosen: enumerate every Table-1-allowed verdict pair and every adaptive branch
rationale: The model allows an adaptive adversary; a single random or always-lie run does not prove the n−1/correctness claim.
quote: A bad chip’s verdict is arbitrary and may be chosen by an adaptive adversary that knows all types, the algorithm, and the history of tests.

gap: Whether to enable Proposition 10 early termination in the base reproduction.
rationale: Algorithm 1 and the GGBBBGG trace run to the end; early termination is an optional optimization.
quote: In particular, BCE may stop and return p.

gap: Whether to apply the parity/even-n optimization that drops one chip at the start.
options: drop one chip when n is even
drop one chip only if n even and g≥b+2
rationale: Algorithm 1 starts with p=x1 and does not discard a chip before the scan; the saving is optional.
quote: Independently, when n is even, the promise gives g ≥b + 2, so one chip may be dropped at the start.

gap: Stack discipline and candidate storage: whether the candidate remains in R or is separate.
rationale: Paper defines C={p}∪R and pushes xi without removing p; pop supplies new p after discarding old p.
quote: We call C = {p}∪R (or ∅if p = ⊥) the retained set.

gap: What to do for n=1 or if p=⊥ at termination on a valid input.
options: return x1 for n=1; raise error if p=⊥
chosen: return x1 for n=1; raise error if p=⊥
rationale: Under g>b, p cannot be ⊥; the paper says p=⊥ certifies a broken promise.
quote: If BCE ends with p = ⊥, the proof of Theorem 5 shows that the promise g > b was violated.

gap: How large an exhaustive simulation to run for the general n−1 bound.
rationale: Small enough for complete adversarial branching, but already covers multiple restarts, backtracks, and bad candidates.
quote: BCE performs at most n −1 tests and runs in O(n) time.

gap: Whether (B,B) should be treated as a consistent same-type outcome because two bad chips can both say B.
rationale: The paper defines consistency by the outcome (G,G); (B,B) is explicitly listed among possible (B,B)-type outcomes and the algorithm routes it to Case 3.
quote: We say a test is consistent if it returns (G, G) and inconsistent otherwise.

gap: Whether to include the Section 6.3 one-directional variant in the base code.
rationale: The paper's main algorithm and target claims are two-sided; the directed scan is an extension.
quote: We also give a variant for the weaker model in which a test yields only one chip’s verdict on the other.
